did_you_know.text: Did you know? The Hebrew word arum means “clever” or “crafty” here, and it sounds like the word for “naked” in verse 7. This is a wordplay in biblical Hebrew.
Did you know? The earlier command forbade eating from the tree, but it did not say that touching it was forbidden. Here, the woman repeats the command in a slightly different form.
Did you know? Fig leaves are large and broad, making them more suitable for covering the body than many other leaves. The fig was also a familiar and important plant in the ancient Near East.
Did you know? In biblical Hebrew, the word zera can mean both literal seed and descendants. So the verse refers not only to the serpent and the woman, but also to their future generations.

Did you know? This verse plays on the Hebrew words adam, “human,” and adamah, “ground,” linking the person to the soil from which he was formed. The wordplay emphasizes humanity’s connection to the earth.

Did you know? The name Chavah, or Eve, is connected with the Hebrew word for “life” and the root meaning “to live.” According to the verse, the name reflects her role as the mother of all living people.

Did you know? The tree of life appeared earlier in the story, and here it explains why the human is not allowed to remain in the garden. The story presents eternal life as something humans cannot simply obtain on their own.

Did you know? In the Bible, cherubim are not baby-like angels with small wings, as they are sometimes shown in art. Elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, they are powerful heavenly beings associated with guarding holy places.
